I read `/data/iceberg/format/spec.md` end-to-end (2,153 lines, in six consecutive chunks: 1–320, 321–680, 681–1060, 1061–1440, 1441–1820, 1821–2153), and verified the last line ("The version of the OGC standard first used here is 1.2.1…", line 2153). Here's the layout and the read path, with line citations.

## The five-level hierarchy

The spec's Overview (lines 79–89) states the core design:

> "This table format tracks individual data files in a table instead of directories" (L83). "Table state is maintained in metadata files… The table metadata file tracks the table schema, partitioning config, custom properties, and snapshots of the table contents. A snapshot represents the state of a table at some time" (L85). "Data files in snapshots are tracked by one or more manifest files that contain a row for each data file… The manifests that make up a snapshot are stored in a manifest list file" (L87–89).

So the hierarchy is: **table metadata → snapshot → manifest list → manifests → data files** (the diagram is referenced at L81).

**1. Table metadata** — stored as JSON, one file per version, committed by an atomic swap (L1136; L85). Every change creates a new metadata file, giving a linear history and preventing lost concurrent writes (L1136). Its fields (Table Metadata Fields, L1140–1141 onward) include `format-version`, `table-uuid`, `location` (table base location), `schemas`/`current-schema-id`, `partition-specs`/`default-spec-id`, `sort-orders`, `properties`, `current-snapshot-id`, and the `snapshots` list — "Valid snapshots are stored as a list in table metadata" (L986). It also carries `refs` (branches/tags) and, in v3+, `next-row-id` for row lineage (L461–470).

**2. Snapshots** — "the state of a table at some point in time, including the set of all data files" (Terms section, ~L143). A snapshot is a small record: `snapshot-id`, `parent-snapshot-id`, `sequence-number`, `timestamp-ms`, and a pointer to a **manifest list** (L953–962; in v1 the pointer could be a flat `manifests` list instead, L962). Note "Snapshots are embedded in table metadata, but the list of manifests for a snapshot are stored in a separate manifest list file" (L1001). A snapshot's data may span many manifests, enabling fast appends, multiple partition specs, and parallel planning (L978–984).

**3. Manifest lists** — one per snapshot, rewritten on every commit attempt (L1003). It is a valid Iceberg data file listing `manifest_file` entries: `manifest_path`, `manifest_length`, `partition_spec_id`, `content` (data vs. deletes), sequence numbers, counts of added/existing/deleted files and rows, and per-partition-field summaries (`field_summary` with `contains_null`, `lower_bound`, `upper_bound`) (manifest list section, L999–1051). These summaries exist so "a reader can avoid scanning all of the manifests in a snapshot when planning a scan" (L1005).

**4. Manifests** — "An immutable Avro file that lists data files or delete files, along with each file's partition data tuple, metrics, and tracking information" (L660). A manifest holds either data files or delete files, not both (L664), and files for a single partition spec (L666). Each entry is a `manifest_entry` with `status` (0 EXISTING / 1 ADDED / 2 DELETED), snapshot id, sequence numbers, and the nested `data_file` struct (L686–697). Deleted entries are informational only and ignored by scans (L691; L1055).

Manifests are **reused across snapshots** to avoid rewriting slow-changing metadata (L87).

**5. Data files** — actual row data (Parquet/ORC/Avro). The `data_file` struct records `file_path`, `file_format`, the `partition` tuple, `record_count`, `file_size_in_bytes`, and column metrics: `column_sizes`, `value_counts`, `null_value_counts`, `lower_bounds`, `upper_bounds`, `split_offsets`, etc. (L713–746). Each content file may be live in at most one manifest entry per snapshot (content file uniqueness, L680–682). Files are also stored with the partition tuple used for filtering (L550) and are immutable once written (L85, L115–119).

## How a reader finds the data files for a query

This is **Scan Planning** (L1053–1132):

1. **Start from a snapshot.** A reader loads table metadata, picks a snapshot — the `current-snapshot-id` for a normal read, or any historical snapshot for time travel (L93 readers "use the snapshot that was current when they load the table metadata"; L1055 "the current snapshot") — and reads its **manifest list**.

2. **Filter manifests.** Manifests that can't contain matches "may be skipped" using the manifest list's file counts and partition summaries (L1057; L1005). This is what makes planning O(1)-ish remote calls rather than O(n) over files (Goals, ~L60).

3. **Convert predicates.** For each remaining manifest, the scan's row predicates are converted to **partition predicates** using the partition spec that wrote that manifest — not the table's current spec (L1059). The conversion is *inclusive*: any row matching the scan predicate must match the partition predicate, so no matching file is skipped, at the cost of some false positives (L1061). Example: for `ts > X` on a `day(ts)`-partitioned table, the inclusive projection is `ts_day >= day(X)` (L1063).

4. **Filter inside manifests by metrics.** Entries are further pruned using per-column `lower_bounds`/`upper_bounds` and counts stored in the manifest `data_file` rows, filtering on "column bounds and counts that are stored by field id" (L1067). Delete files are pruned with the same logic — a delete file whose deletes can't overlap the query can be ignored (L1067–1068).

5. **Build the file set.** The surviving entries name the actual data files. Delete files and deletion vectors that match are applied to the data files at read time, with scope rules (older data files, same partition, matching sequence numbers — L1069–1091). The resulting data files (plus the applicable deletes) are what the reader reads.

The crucial property throughout: readers never scan directories or list objects — they navigate a metadata tree (metadata → snapshot → manifest list → manifests → data file paths), pruning at each level with compact statistics so planning cost doesn't grow with file count.
